newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka stocks at 28-month high, to rise more.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka stocks at 28-month high, to rise more.

text.p: Sri Lankan stocks, which rose to a 28-month high on Wednesday, are expected to post further gains in the short-term, but at a slower pace, analysts said.
The Colombo Stock Exchange all share index closed at 860.1 on Wednesday, a level not seen since early March 1995.
"The upward momentum, which began in January on improved sentiment, was boosted in July by exceptionally good interm results to June," said Nanda Nair, head of research at brokerage John Keells.
The index has risen 253.1 points so far in 1997 and has gained 68.2 points in July alone.
"The index should continue to rise, but upward momentum should slow down, as second-half results are seen rising at a gentler pace," Nair added.

Analysts say first half 1997 results were sharply higher than in the same period in 1996, which was a dismal year due to a severe drought. It led to power cuts which badly hit industry and agriculture and depressed GDP (gross domestic product) growth to 3.8 percent from 5.5.
"Corporte results to June 1997 were better-than-expected, mainly as they were coming from a low base in 1996," Nair said.
Ten leading firms which have released interim results to June 1997, have shown an average profit growth of 66 percent each, compared to a contraction in the same period in 1996.
Some analysts said the all share index might continue to rise at the same pace, as improved investor sentiment which led the up-swing, would bear real fruit only in the second half.
"I do not see the upward momentum slowing down at all," said Priyal Perera, head of research at Ceybank Unit Trust.

"Officials in corporates and banks say they expect the real fruits of improved investor sentiment to come through in terms of higher turnover and increased demand for long-term credit etc in the second half," he said.

Investor sentiment rose as interest rates fell due to improved money supply, the government's landslide victory at local polls in March and a subsequent agreement with the main opposition party to work jointly to solve the island's ethnic conflict.

The war, between the Sri Lankan government and Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels (LTTE) fighting for an independent state in the north and east, consumes nearly six percent of the country's GDP.
A recent Reuter poll of seven leading local brokers said the all share index could end the year close to 950 points.
Analysts say privatisation of a 35 percent holding in Sri Lanka Telecom and the government's holding in a bank should also push up the all share index a notch or two.
"The index should zig-zag its way and end 1997 between 950 to 975 points without a problem, all things being equal," said Nouzab Fareed, head of reserch at Allied Phillips Securities.
Analysts said they didn't think the index would break into a raging bull run, mainly because of the continuing ethnic war.
They noted that foreign investor sentiment and tourism were both hit in 1996 after the LTTE bombed the Central Bank and a crowded commuter train.
